claims.text: The onset and progression of melting in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are governed by surface-induced atomic segregation.
Surface segregation lowers the local melting point at FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticle surfaces.
Surface premelting propagates inward as temperature increases.
The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are fully crystalline and solid.
The starting nanoparticles have a nominally homogeneous elemental distribution.
Lower-temperature pre-annealing minimizes surface segregation in otherwise identical nanoparticles.
Lower-melting-point elements migrate to and become enriched at the nanoparticle surfaces.
Surface energy minimization drives elemental segregation at free nanoparticle surfaces.
The segregated surface has a lower local melting point than the nanoparticle interior.
Segregation-induced melting-point depression produces a thin liquid-like surface layer.
Formation of the liquid-like surface layer enables the liquid phase to propagate gradually into the interior during further heating.
Initial melting will appear as a liquid-like surface layer below the bulk alloy melting point.
Melting will progress inward as temperature increases.
Pre-annealed nanoparticles with reduced segregation will exhibit delayed surface premelting relative to untreated nanoparticles.
The proposed behavior applies under inert atmosphere and controlled heating when nanoparticle surface-to-volume effects are significant.
Sufficiently large particles may display bulk-like behavior rather than the proposed surface-dominated response.
Oxidation may alter surface energies and cause deviations from the proposed behavior.
The melting-temperature shift and surface-liquid-layer extent depend on nanoparticle size, initial compositional homogeneity, and heating conditions.

contradictions.description: The intervention specifies heating to above the nominal bulk melting point, whereas the stated temperature span ends at 1.0 times the bulk melting temperature and therefore does not include temperatures above it.

Pre-annealing is asserted to minimize surface segregation, while the mechanism states that surface-energy minimization drives segregation at free surfaces. No annealing or quenching pathway is provided to explain why thermal pre-treatment would reduce rather than promote the proposed segregation.
